articles.title: How a police officer’s obsession with his ex-lover led to double murder
articles.summary: Driven by “jealousy,” the police officer killed his TV presenter ex-boyfriend and his new partner – then told “fantastical” lies to cover it up, the prosecution said.
articles.body: Taylor Swift’s “No Body, No Crime” was playing as Senior Constable Beau Lamarre-Condon drove a white hire van with a friend two hours south of Sydney, toward a rural property where he knew of a dam. It was hot, and two corpses hidden inside surfboard bags in the back of the van were starting to decompose. He was planning to submerge the bodies in water, to remove any trace of the TV presenter and his new partner. It’d already been two days since an encounter at an Australian home that Lamarre-Condon claimed had ended in their unintended deaths. Prosecutors would soon call it murder. In handwritten testimony presented to the court, Lamarre-Condon told police that the passenger in his van – known by the alias Elizabeth Kennedy – had told him not to turn himself in. “You can’t. They won’t believe you,” Lamarre-Condon claims she said, according to his written testimony. “I watch a lot of crime documentaries, I know what we have to do.” “We have to hide the bodies.” The cop and the TV presenter Lamarre-Condon and Jesse Baird were in their late 20s when they met in Sydney in October 2022. Both went to the same bars and used gay dating apps. It was almost inevitable that their paths would cross. At the time, Baird was working as a presenter for Australia’s Network 10, having graduated from children’s programs to become a roving reporter on breakfast TV, sometimes filling in as co-host and interviewing celebrities on the red carpet. Lamarre-Condon was a police officer with expensive taste that he satisfied with a side hustle as a swimwear entrepreneur, marketing sexy bathing suits for Sydney’s gay men, and reselling Hermès bags that he bought in Paris. Before joining the police force, he also dabbled in celebrity blogging, posting images of himself with stars including Taylor Swift, Lady Gaga and Harry Styles. By February 2023, the two men had been on a few dates. A year later, both Baird, 26, and his new boyfriend, Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies, 29, would be dead – with Lamarre-Condon accused of their murder. Lawyers for Lamarre-Condon claimed he shot Baird in self-defense, and that Davies fatally shot himself in the head as they wrestled over the gun. Prosecutors argued in a two-month trial that Lamarre-Condon had become obsessed with the presenter and set out to murder him, killing Davies to eliminate a witness and telling “fantastical, elaborate lies” to cover his tracks. He pleaded not guilty to two murder charges. A promising romance In early 2023, Lamarre-Condon was giddy with excitement over the presenter’s long-term-partner potential, texting a friend to tell her about his new romance. “Last night was cute. He made me dinner and we just chilled out. Our intimacy and sex is getting more and more intense and he keeps going on about it. Arghh haha…” he said in the message. She replied: “Oooohhh he’s really enjoying it! I don’t know why he won’t commit to you tbh…” Even then, signs were emerging of the police officer’s jealous streak. On a weekend away in March, Lamarre-Condon said he covertly checked Baird’s phone to see if he was dating other men. And while he was scrolling, he quickly “unfollowed” two or three people from Baird’s Instagram account. While Lamarre-Condon saw a future with Baird, in mid-April, the presenter said that he wasn’t ready for anything serious. The two men parted ways, wishing each other well in text messages, and Lamarre-Condon said he stepped away to “let the romantic feelings settle.” But within a few months, they were back on. It was a casual, non-exclusive relationship, but Lamarre-Condon again wanted to know who else Baird was seeing. In August 2023, as Baird slept, Lamarre-Condon broke into his home and stole his phone and wallet. As he unplugged the phone from the charger by the bed, the cord dropped, waking Baird. Dazed and alarmed, Baird chased the intruder down the street but failed to catch him. Lamarre-Condon said the next time they went out, it was apparent that Baird did not suspect he was the intruder. In November 2023, Lamarre-Condon posted an Instagram story with settings so that only Baird’s new love interest would see it. It was a photo of flowers with the caption: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these,” meant to imply the flowers were from Baird. The love interest was puzzled and asked Baird about it. Baird then posed the question to Lamarre-Condon, who initially vehemently denied any knowledge of what he was referring to. “Jesse, I’m literally sitting here in tears trying to piece this all together….” he wrote in a long, emotional text message exceeding 800 words. “This shit is simply out of character for me because I would never even have the thought to want to do anything to betray your trust or think of doing this…” Lovesick and contrite, Lamarre-Condon ultimately admitted posting the photo – and conceded that he accessed Baird’s phone without permission. For Baird, the deception was too much, and he told Lamarre-Condon not to contact him again. Two days later, Lamarre-Condon told his mother in a text message that he couldn’t “eat or sleep.” He asked to borrow her car so he could go to Baird’s house with flowers to clear the air. But on the way, he saw Baird walking down the street, holding hands with a new boyfriend. It was clear Baird had moved on. Lamarre-Condon’s reliance on his female friends for comfort provided police with more evidence of his growing fury over Baird’s rejection of his advances. He sent a friend a draft of another 800-word text message that was later submitted as evidence. The message, in part, read: “It’s very clear you have commitment issues and that’s fine, just own that from the start instead of literally playing mind games with people’s lives, emotions and feelings then making them look like the problem. You need to also take accountability Jesse…” However, a few days later he asked another friend to send Baird a 1,600-word text message that tried to explain away his behavior by revealing that he had a cancer diagnosis – which was not true. Three shots fired On the day of the shootings in February 2024, Lamarre-Condon’s alarm was set for 4:30 a.m. Within 35 minutes, he’d started his Tesla and activated a burner phone. He drove for 20 minutes to a Sydney suburb six miles away, where CCTV video shows he parked and picked up an SUV his mother had rented the day before. From 6 a.m., for almost five hours, his burner phone pinged a cellphone tower near the Paddington home that Baird shared with housemates. In that time, Lamarre-Condon could be seen on a neighbor’s security camera, hanging around the SUV. Lamarre-Condon would later claim in court he was waiting for Baird and his housemates to leave, so he could sneak into the home to retrieve a $16,000 Cartier ring, a surfboard and shirts worth thousands of dollars that he’d left behind during their on-and-off fling. “Just before 9 a.m., I thought this is not worth it. I couldn’t be certain he’s not there,” Lamarre-Condon testified. The car is seen driving away, then Lamarre-Condon returns on foot, dressed in a high-visibility jacket and a black helmet with a tinted visor. Lamarre-Condon said he’d stolen the jacket and helmet on impulse from a bike parked nearby so he could disguise himself as a food delivery driver. He’d been worried Baird would accuse him of harassment, as he’d already told him not to contact him. He thought that if he knocked on the door and Baird was home, he wouldn’t be able to see his face. “I could just say ‘wrong address’ in a different voice and walk away without any verbal argument or confrontation with Jesse. And if he wasn’t home, I could enter with the spare key that he got cut for me and go in and get my belongings,” he told the court. He left his two phones in his car and was carrying his police firearm in his backpack. He said he took his gun to Baird’s home because he couldn’t leave it in his car; police rules stipulate that firearms can’t be left unsecured. Dressed as the food delivery driver, the police officer was seen walking out of shot. Several minutes later, two shots ring out, according to sound from a neighbor’s security camera. Someone uses Luke Davies’ phone to call emergency services, but all the operator hears is “F**k off” before the line is cut. A third blast rings out. Less than a minute has passed between the first and last shot. The former constable admitted shooting Baird but claimed it was in self-defense after his former lover mistook him for an intruder and slashed at him with a knife. Lamarre-Condon’s version of events told of two separate struggles. He said when Baird saw the helmeted intruder in his house, he yelled, “We’re getting robbed! We’re getting robbed! We’re getting robbed!” Lamarre-Condon said he tried to identify himself: “It’s Beau, it’s me, calm the f**k down.” But Baird lunged at him with a knife and pinned him up against the wall, Lamarre-Condon said, swinging the knife within centimeters of his throat. “I realized, shit, if he drives that into my throat, I’m going to be dead,” Lamarre-Condon told the court. Lamarre-Condon said he reached for his firearm, and aimed for his right shoulder, to force him to drop the knife. “I could have shot him in the center of the chest to kill him, but I did not want to kill Jesse,” he told the court. Another shot was fired as they struggled over the gun, Lamarre-Condon said. That one hit Baird in the head, and it was fatal. Lamarre-Condon said he then tried to call emergency services from Davies’ phone, but Davies had picked up his gun and was in the hallway, threatening to shoot him. “He just told me, ‘I’m gonna f**king shoot you.’ Now he’s raising the gun towards my head, and that’s when again my police training kicked in,” Lamarre-Condon testified. He claimed Davies accidentally shot himself as they wrestled over the firearm. Lamarre-Condon said he wanted to call police but “couldn’t take the risk” that they’d accuse him of shooting a witness. The prosecution said that’s exactly what he did. Prosecutors said Lamarre-Condon didn’t know Davies was in the house when he killed Baird, and that he shot Davies through a door, as he tried to call for help. Suicidal or homicidal? In the weeks leading up to the shooting, the police officer went on dates, to the beach, cafes, a recovery spa, and a weekend acting class with different friends. He was seen on CCTV two days before the incident, shopping with a friend for a surfboard bag. They laughed as he jokingly held up the bag against his friend to measure its size. Lamarre-Condon told the court the video and text messages didn’t capture the whole picture. He said he’d been bullied in the police force and was so traumatized by work that he’d previously attempted to kill himself. He said he’d checked out his police pistol before the shootings because he had intended to take his own life. Brett Hatfield SC, the crown prosecutor, put it to him that on the day of the shooting, “You weren’t suicidal; you were homicidal, weren’t you?” “I was not,” Lamarre-Condon replied. Hiding the bodies In the handwritten statement, Lamarre-Condon told investigators that the day after the shooting he reached out on Signal, the encrypted messaging app, to a friend – the woman granted court-ordered anonymity under the alias Elizabeth Kennedy. When they arrived at the farm, in the small town of Bungonia, the gate was locked, so the pair went to another hardware store to find a tool to break in. A shop assistant testified that they told him they were staying on a friend’s farm and had locked themselves out. He recommended using an angle grinder to cut the lock. Once inside the property, Lamarre-Condon said they drove to a dam. After their attempts to sink Davies’ body failed, Lamarre-Condon said he dropped Kennedy home. Kennedy testified that none of that was true – she said that she didn’t know about the shootings, or that there were bodies in the van. Kennedy said she thought Lamarre-Condon was picking her up for lunch, but he kept driving. Lamarre-Condon had the windows open, and the air-conditioning turned up. She said the van smelt like cleaning products, and it was Lamarre-Condon’s idea to play the ghoulishly apt Taylor Swift song as they drove. He’d told her he needed to break into his friend’s farm to “save” some cattle that were going to escape. After they’d cut the lock, she said she waited at the gate for about 30 to 40 minutes for him to return. “I didn’t know anything,” she told the court. “I’m five foot and weigh 55 kilos (120 pounds), so I don’t think I could carry a body even if I tried.” Kennedy, along with two other witnesses, agreed to give evidence in the trial on the condition that it would not be used against them in any future criminal proceedings. Lamarre-Condon’s defense said, as such, their evidence should be treated with caution and submitted that nothing Kennedy said could be trusted. Cleaning the scene The deaths of Baird and Davies shocked Sydney’s gay community, and the alleged involvement of a serving officer sent tremors through the ranks of the New South Wales Police Force. Lamarre-Condon repeatedly referred to his job throughout his testimony – using it to explain how he knew how to disarm someone pointing a gun at him – and also to argue that the killings weren’t planned. He said he worked in the NSW Police Youth Command, guiding troubled youth, and could have easily obtained an untraceable firearm. Furthermore, he could have found someone else to do it. “You can pay a youth gang $30,000 to go commit a murder,” he told the court. Lamarre-Condon’s defense team maintained the police officer “panicked considerably” – his experience in law enforcement had taught him how it would look. So, he set about cleaning the scene, stuffing the men’s bodies into separate surfboard bags, scrubbing away the blood, and dumping their blood-covered belongings in an industrial waste bin 17 miles away. In between shopping for supplies to conceal the bodies, Lamarre-Condon went out with a friend for sushi, texted another friend to make plans for the weekend, and attended a pre-booked hospital appointment for minor surgery. Lamarre-Condon claimed he didn’t know it, but on the day after the murder, Baird had been due to move out of his share house. Someone else was waiting to move in, and his housemates were confused as to why Baird had left food in the fridge and toiletries in the bathroom. One admonished him in a group chat for not clearing out his stuff. Lamarre-Condon still had Baird’s phone and – posing as Baird – sent a text to the group, telling them he couldn’t pick up his possessions, because he was going to Perth, thousands of miles away in Western Australia. At the same time, Lamarre-Condon used his own phone to text an acquaintance in Perth, asking for a favor. He wanted to post her a phone that she’d switch on briefly before throwing it into a body of water, she told the court. The phone never arrived. Instead, Lamarre-Condon told the court he threw Baird’s phone off a bridge into a river himself. “I obviously did it because I didn’t want to have any evidence of Jesse’s phone on me,” he said. Getting to the truth It wasn’t until Friday – four days after the shooting – that Lamarre-Condon walked into Sydney’s Bondi Beach police station and handed himself in. That weekend, as he sat in a police cell accused of double murder, his colleagues searched for the missing men’s bodies. Based on information provided by Lamarre-Condon, they eventually found the bodies covered with rocks and branches near the fenceline of a Greek Orthodox monastery some 12 miles from the Bungonia farm. Forensic analysis of the bodies revealed more evidence that would later back the prosecution case. The first bullet that hit Baird was likely fired from behind, and the trajectory suggested he was crouching or ducking at the time, according to an expert witness. He wasn’t hit in the shoulder, but through the base of the neck, likely incapacitating him, the witness said. The second shot went through his head. Ballistic evidence also suggests that Lamarre-Condon fired a bullet through a door that hit and killed Davies. The prosecution pointed to Lamarre-Condon’s alleged admission to a friend in the hours after the shooting that he shot one person in the head and a second through a door. The same friend agreed to wear a police wire last December when he visited Lamarre-Condon in prison, and in audio recordings played to the jury, the officer was heard telling his friend that he had misheard or misunderstood what he had said about the second person. “The truth is, you misheard it,” Lamarre-Condon was heard saying. “I don’t believe you’re a liar, and I know you’re not, right? However, I know that humans… get shit wrong. Hear shit wrong.” When questioned about the exchange on the stand, Lamarre-Condon denied suggestions that he had tried to pressure his friend into changing his testimony. “I just want the truth to be told,” Lamarre-Condon told the court. “This was my life. I just want the truth to be told. I need to take accountability for what I have done, which I have, and it’s manslaughter.” The prosecution said the truth was that Lamarre-Condon had become obsessed with Baird and, motivated by “sexual jealousy,” set out to murder him. “You knew what you did, and what you did was totally inconsistent with self-defense or an accident, wasn’t it?” prosecutor Hatfield put to Lamarre-Condon in cross-examination. “I disagree,” he replied. “It was murder, plain and simple. You murdered Jesse Baird, didn’t you?” “I did not.” “And then you murdered Luke Davies, shooting him through the door to eliminate him as a witness, didn’t you?” “I did not.” Just two hours after retiring to consider their verdicts, the 12-member jury found the former police officer guilty of two counts of murder. The fast, unanimous decision suggests they needed little convincing. Lamarre-Condon, now 31, will be sentenced in March. He’ll likely spend decades in prison.

articles.title: WHO chief urges end to US fuel blockade on Cuba
articles.summary: UN allocates $2m for immunisation and medical equipment as Cuban healthcare struggles with critical shortages.
articles.body:
World Health ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called for the lifting of a US fuel blockade on Cuba , as shortages dent the island’s once vaunted healthcare system.

Tedros warned that the sanctions were endangering the lives of children on Tuesday, during a ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠visit to Cuba that included tours of several healthcare facilities in Havana.

“The intensification ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Tedros said.

During his three-day visit , the United Nations health agency’s top official said his organisation would contribute $2m to help strengthen Cuba’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌national immunisation programme and provide essential medical equipment to healthcare facilities.

The UN has repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, calling the US blockade a violation of international law and the human rights of all Cubans.

Cuba’s government says the measures ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠led to daily power outages lasting 20 hours ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠or more, critical shortages of medicines and surgical supplies, and a decline in health indicators, such as infant mortality rates.

Tedros met with Cuba’s President Miguel Diaz-Canel on Tuesday to discuss the country’s health needs.

“We agreed on the need to prioritise essential health services and time-sensitive interventions, particularly for children,” Tedros wrote in a post on X.

“Fuel restrictions and sanctions affecting the purchase of medical products are severely impacting the health system that Cuban doctors have built over decades.”

Tedros said during a news conference that Cuba’s life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.

The 2025 figures predate the imposition by the administration of US President Donald Trump of a fuel blockade and stiff sanctions against a ‌number of Cuban officials and entities in January.

Washington argues the energy blockade is intended to push for ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠political change on the island and says that exports of food and medicine are subject ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠to legal exemptions.

An annual non-binding resolution calling for an end to a US embargo on the island has ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌passed ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌in favour of Cuba in the UN General Assembly by wide margins every year since 1992.

articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports to Spain after lengthy US legal battle
articles.summary: US Senator Chris Van Hollen hails Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s safe departure to Spain as a ‘free man’.
articles.body:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year as part of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has self-deported to Spain.

Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, voluntarily departed on Tuesday after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, The Associated Press reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while pressing for his release from Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT, said Abrego Garcia is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man”.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen, who is vying for Senate majority leader, said in a statement posted on X.

Abrego Garcia, 31, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison notorious for abusive conditions and alleged use of torture.

The Trump administration, at the time, described Abrego Garcia’s deportation as an “administrative error”. However, the administration initially refused to seek his return, arguing that Abrego Garcia was a member of the MS-13 gang despite having no criminal record at the time of his removal.

In June 2025 , the Trump administration brought him back after facing public pressure and a court order, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee .

The Tennessee case was dismissed by a federal judge in May, though the government appealed it in August .

Abrego Garcia had said that if he must be deported, he would prefer to be sent to Costa Rica, but Todd Lyons, the former acting director of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said that deporting him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States” in a March 2026 memo.

Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the US has spent government resources and political capital negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.

The memo came despite a US agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.

Abrego Garcia has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager.

In 2019, an immigration judge issued an order saying that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family.

The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.

articles.title: Nearly 6 decades after teen was killed while leaving job, Canada authorities know who did it
articles.summary: Authorities in Canada have identified a man accused of killing a Canadian teen nearly six decades ago, police said Monday.
articles.body: Authorities in Canada have identified a man accused of killing a Canadian teen nearly six decades ago, police said Monday. Michael Joseph Moore, who died in 2018, was responsible for the 1968 death of Jacqueline “Jacky” Dunleavy, 16, according to the London Police Service in Ontario. Moore, who worked as a firefighter for nearly three decades, was identified through genetic genealogy, officials said at a news conference Monday. The forensic technique combines modern DNA analysis with traditional genealogical research. If Moore was alive today, the agency said in a statement, he would have been arrested and charged in connection with the teen’s death. “Publicly identifying Moore provides an accurate historical record and answers that Jackie’s family and the community have sought for decades,” the agency said. In a statement read at the news conference, Dunleavy’s family thanked law enforcement and said they hope the techniques used to solve her death can be used with other cold cases. Authorities did not identify a possible motive, and a possible connection between Moore and Dunleavy remained unclear. The high school sophomore was last seen on the evening of Jan. 9, 1968, leaving her job at a variety store in London, roughly 120 miles northeast of Detroit. Dunleavy was found dead at a school 90 minutes later, the police service said. She had a head injury, according to the authorities, and her cause of death was determined to be strangulation. Despite what the agency described as an extensive investigation, the case remained unsolved, and efforts in the decades that followed did not reveal her killer. “The investigators who worked on Jackie’s homicide in 1968 did everything they could with the investigative and forensic tools available to them at the time,” Det. Sgt. Micah Bourdeau of the London Police Service said in a statement. “The evidence they carefully collected and preserved ultimately allowed investigators decades later to continue that work.” Recently, a Texas-based DNA lab conducted specialized testing using that evidence and investigators were able to develop a family tree that helped identify Moore, the police service said. After conducting additional interviews, gathering new evidence and obtaining comparison DNA samples, Moore was identified as the man responsible for the teen’s killing, the agency said. Moore, who was 25 at the time, had moved to Canada from Ireland in 1967, authorities said. He worked as a firefighter for 28 years but did not have that job until after Dunleavy’s death, Det. Mike Budzyn of the London Police Service told reporters. At the time he retired, Moore was a captain. His family was shocked by the revelation, Budzyn said, and “expressed their hope that these findings will provide long-awaited answers for Jackie’s family.”

articles.title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
articles.summary: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.
articles.body:
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing .

There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."

"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."

On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China .

articles.title: Judge denies bail for former Penn State fraternity brother at center of drug bust
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday denied bail to the former Penn State student authorities say was at the center of a drug trafficking ring at the university, ordering him to remain in custody pending trial.
articles.body: A federal judge on Tuesday denied bail to the former Penn State student authorities say was at the center of a drug trafficking ring at the university, ordering him to remain in custody pending trial. Agostino Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was arrested and charged with one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distributing cocaine earlier this month. Federal prosecutors accused Abbatiello, a former member of Sigma Chi, of conspiring to sell at least five kilograms of cocaine between January 2023 and December 2024 in State College, Pennsylvania, according to an indictment. Abbatiello’s conspiracy charge carries a minimum of 10 years in prison and a maximum of life. He has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. “The court’s decision to deny bail is incredibly disappointing, and in our view, fundamentally wrong,” Abbatiello’s lawyer, Edward J. Rymsza, said in an email. “We vigorously disagree with the ruling and will be appealing.” Federal prosecutors filed a motion on Wednesday in support of Abbatiello’s detention. Officials argued Abbatiello poses a danger to the community and is a flight risk. The Justice Department also argued that the “weight of the evidence” warrants his detention, noting that investigators “utilized cooperating witnesses, controlled drug purchases, search warrants, and interviews to dismantle this drug trafficking organization.” “The evidence continues to grow stronger,” the motion reads. On Sunday, Abbatiello’s attorney filed a brief opposing Abbatiello’s detention. The attorney, Edward J. Rymsza, argued that Abbatiello “has already demonstrated” he will “appear and obey the law while on release.” State officials arrested and charged Abbatiello in connection with the same alleged drug trafficking scheme in August. In the state case, Abbatiello was charged with felony corrupt organizations, conspiracy and dealing in proceeds of unlawful activity. Rymsza said his client voluntarily surrendered to state authorities, has appeared at scheduled court proceedings, and has been out on $250,000 bail without violating it. According to the brief in opposition, Abbatiello had been living with his parents and siblings at their home on Long Island, New York. Thirteen other people were arrested and charged by state officials in connection with the alleged drug ring. The other defendants include current and former students and the father of a former student, and they face various counts. Penn State announced that it will no longer recognize the other fraternity officials said was involved in the alleged drug ring, Delta Upsilon, hours after the DOJ announced Abbatiello’s charges. Sigma Chi already lost its recognition.

articles.title: This nation had a security pact with China. It’s just signed a deal with a US ally instead
articles.summary: Australia and Solomon Islands signed a security pact on Wednesday that makes Canberra the country’s defense partner of choice, marking a shift for the Pacific archipelago that signed a similar deal with China only four years ago.
articles.body: Australia and Solomon Islands signed a security pact on Wednesday that makes Canberra the country’s defense partner of choice, marking a shift for the Pacific archipelago that signed a similar deal with China only four years ago. Under the deal, Australia will support the expansion and development of Solomon Islands’ police and border force, while Honiara will deny any request from a foreign power to establish military or security bases on its territory, the leaders of the countries said in a joint statement. “Australia is proud to be the Solomon Islands’ main security partner, and that’s a responsibility that we take seriously,” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a press conference in Canberra with his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale. The pact is a victory for Canberra, which is battling China for influence in the region and recently signed similar agreements with Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji. The wide-ranging treaty includes Australian funding for investment in infrastructure and education, improved visa arrangements for Solomon Islanders, and requires Honiara to consult Australia on the development of critical infrastructure. It signals a significant shift by Wale, a long-time China critic who had appeared to soften his stance in recent years. “Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done,” Wale said at the press conference. Wale was highly critical of the 2022 security deal with China, echoing the United States and other Pacific nations, saying it would upset regional security and could jeopardise relationships with existing partners. But in 2025 he led a delegation to Beijing, where he praised China’s economic development and said his party supported the one-China principle. Australian media reported on Wednesday that Solomon Islands’ pact with China had been scrapped, though Wale declined to comment on the status of the deal, citing a non-disclosure agreement. A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “I think this deal, coupled with indications that Solomon Islands will let the China deal lapse, goes beyond the success of the previous deals” which Australia has struck in the region, said Connor Graham, a research fellow in the Pacific Islands program at Sydney-based think tank the Lowy Institute. “It is a blow to Chinese security ambitions in the Pacific certainly.”

articles.title: The Gambia election: Can the next president deliver on a decade of promise?
articles.summary: Gambians head to the polls amid economic hardship and unfulfilled promises of reform and justice.
articles.body:
Banjul, The Gambia – As Gambians prepare to vote on December 5, unemployment, rising living costs, unreliable public services and delayed justice are testing the country’s democratic transition. Nearly a decade after Yahya Jammeh’s departure, voters are asking whether the next president can deliver the change they were promised.

For Sosseh Jagne, the election is about more than who occupies the State House. It is about whether the next government can create conditions in which Gambians can earn a living.

Jagne established Ya Anna’s Catering in 2020 and expanded it into a restaurant in early 2025. But frequent electricity outages have disrupted her business, affecting food preparation, refrigeration and customer service. Between August and October, she said, power cuts sometimes lasted 19 hours or longer.

She estimates that spoiled food cost her more than 40,000 Gambian dalasis ($532). She has also stopped selling homemade iced juices because she cannot guarantee they will remain properly chilled.

“Electricity is not a luxury; it is a necessity for people’s everyday lives and, especially, for businesses that depend on it to operate,” she told Al Jazeera.

Her experience reflects the pressures facing households and businesses as President Adama Barrow seeks a third term. He is one of eight candidates in the December 5 election, according to the Independent Electoral Commission. Barrow came to power in 2017 after defeating Jammeh, who ruled the country for 22 years.

For many young Gambians, the central question is where they can find work.

The 2025 Gambia Labour Force Survey puts overall unemployment at 8.3 percent, up from 7.6 percent in 2022–23. Among people aged 15 to 35, unemployment stands at 11.5 percent. The survey also found that 41.3 percent of young people in that age group were neither employed nor in education or training.

For 26-year-old Maram Mendy, a graduate of the University of The Gambia, finding a job has become increasingly discouraging. Her parents sacrificed to finance her education, making her inability to find work particularly difficult.

“I’m now fed up with looking for a job,” she told Al Jazeera.

She said employers frequently demand previous experience, leaving graduates caught in a cycle: They cannot get a job without experience, but cannot gain experience without employment.

For 28-year-old Buba Sanneh, unemployed since graduating in 2023, the frustration has prompted thoughts of travelling to Europe through irregular migration, commonly known as the backway.

For Hakeem Touray, the search for opportunities abroad has already cost his family dearly. His elder brother, Bob, was 27 when he attempted the journey to Europe in 2021. He died trying to cross the Mediterranean Sea.

Hakeem said the loss highlighted the consequences of unemployment, poverty and limited opportunities at home.

The risks are reflected in figures cited by UN Special Rapporteur Morris Tidball-Binz, following his visit to The Gambia in October 2026. In his end-of-mission statement, he said independent sources had reported that 1,603 Gambians died attempting irregular migration in 2024 and 893 in 2025, most of them at sea. Separately, the International Organization for Migration had recorded at least 408 Gambians missing along migration routes since 2014.

For families, these are not simply statistics but lives lost and loved ones whose fate remains uncertain.

Economic hardship extends beyond unemployment. According to figures published by the Gambia Bureau of Statistics, 53.4 percent of the population – about 1.1 million people – lived below the national poverty line in 2020. The rate was particularly high in rural areas, at about 76 percent, compared with 34 percent in urban areas.

At Bakoteh Market, 38-year-old vegetable seller Fatoumatta Jawara said rising prices have made supporting her family increasingly difficult. She also wants affordable healthcare to become a priority.

“Survival is becoming harder with each passing day. We need a president who will improve our lives for the better,” she told Al Jazeera.

Nearby, 22-year-old Isatou Ceesay, a mother of two, said she had grown tired of politicians’ promises.

“All they do is promise, and after the election you don’t hear from them again. We are tired of their endless promises,” she said.

Security is another concern, particularly in communities near Senegal’s Casamance region. Instability in the neighbouring region has raised concerns about the safety of border communities and the livelihoods that depend on cross-border movement.

For families affected by abuses under Jammeh, the 2017 change of government brought hopes of accountability. Nearly a decade later, many are still waiting.

Sainabou Camara Lowe was 17 when security forces violently suppressed student demonstrations in April 2000, leaving more than a dozen students dead. She survived, but sustained a spinal injury that required two operations.

Now 43 and widowed, she raises five children while struggling with limited mobility. Although she received about 900,000 dalasis ($11,970) through the reparations process, she said the payment had done little to ease her family’s hardship.

“We are forgotten as victims and continue to wallow in pain and poverty,” she told Al Jazeera.

Kebba Jome, national coordinator of the Gambia Centre for Victims of Human Rights Violations, said fewer than 25 percent of the 263 recommendations made by the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission had been fully implemented.

A special tribunal to prosecute alleged crimes committed under Jammeh is expected to begin hearings early next year, Jome said. He argued that the next president would have a responsibility to ensure the accountability process moves forward.

For Muhammed and Fatoumatta Sandeng, the children of opposition activist Ebrima Solo Sandeng, justice remains central to the promises made after Jammeh’s departure. Their father died in state custody in April 2016 after being tortured, according to the findings of the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission.

They want the next administration to implement the commission’s recommendations and ensure those responsible for abuses are brought to justice.

“Victims have been waiting, victims are dying,” Fatoumatta said. “Justice is long overdue.”

These demands come against a backdrop of unfinished political reform. A central pledge of the post-Jammeh transition, replacing the 1997 Constitution, remains unfulfilled.

The 2020 Draft Constitution, drawn up after a public review process, proposed a two-term limit for presidents, among other institutional changes. It failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the National Assembly in September 2020. Disagreements over the draft included whether Barrow’s first term should count towards the proposed limit. Barrow blamed opposition resistance for its failure and has said he would revisit constitutional reform if re-elected.

His main challenger, Ousainou Darboe, leader of the United Democratic Party (UDP), has pledged to reintroduce the 2020 draft constitution within his first 100 days in office. His party’s 2026 manifesto also commits him to serving one five-year term.

The manifesto sets out proposals for institutional and security-sector reform, reducing the budget of the Office of the President, tackling public debt and improving the delivery of services, including healthcare, education, electricity and water.

Other candidates include Talib Ahmed Bensouda, the former mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and independent candidate Almameh Gibba, who has said he would facilitate Jammeh’s return if elected.

Former Vice President Isatou Touray is seeking to become the country’s first woman president. Campaigning under the symbol of a broom, she has promised a new constitution and improvements in living conditions.

Political scientist Essa Njie said the election would be shaped by economic conditions, candidates’ personalities and party loyalty. While unemployment, the cost of living and corruption are important concerns, he said, some voters would also make their choices along ethnic, religious and political lines.

The next administration will face the challenge of turning campaign commitments into reforms amid institutional constraints and competing political interests.

For many Gambians, December 5 is about whether the next five years will bring tangible improvements to everyday life.

Jagne wants reliable electricity to keep her business running, Mendy wants an opportunity to enter the workforce, and Sanneh wants a future that does not require risking his life on the backway. Market sellers want to feed their children and afford healthcare. Families of victims want accountability and the assurance that their loved ones have not been forgotten.

Nearly a decade after Jammeh’s departure, these expectations remain central to The Gambia’s democratic journey. Whoever wins will inherit not only the responsibility of governing the country but also the burden of promises that remain unfulfilled.

For Hakeem Touray, whose brother died trying to reach Europe, the stakes are particularly personal.

“Our young people are not necessarily running away from The Gambia; many are running away from hopelessness,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday strongly condemned the Houthi attack on a tower in Saudi Arabia's Financial District in Riyadh that left 11 people injured,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday strongly condemned the Houthi attack on a tower in Saudi Arabia's Financial District in Riyadh that left 11 people injured, including two Indian nationals, and called for an immediate halt to strikes targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in the Kingdom.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) said the attacks endangered civilian lives, violated Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and threatened regional security and stability. It also reaffirmed India's support for Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its territorial integrity and the safety of its citizens and residents.In an official statement, the MEA said, "We strongly condemn the attack on one of the towers of the financial district in Riyadh on November 24 as well as the continued attacks targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."Confirming that two Indians were among those injured, the ministry said the Indian Embassy in Riyadh was providing assistance to the victims and their families."Two Indians are among those injured in the attack on Riyadh financial district. The Embassy of India in Riyadh is providing all possible assistance to the injured and their families," the statement added.The MEA further said, "These attacks seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability. We call for immediate cessation of such attacks."Reaffirming India's support for the Kingdom, the ministry said, "We also reiterate our firm solidarity with the people and Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and reaffirm our unwavering support to the Kingdom in safeguarding its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the security and safety of its citizens and residents. We earnestly hope that peace and normalcy will return to the region at the earliest."11 injured in attack on Riyadh towerThe condemnation followed a statement by Saudi Arabia's General Directorate of Civil Defence confirming that 11 people were injured after a tower in Riyadh's Financial Centre was targeted in what it described as a terrorist attack by Yemen's Houthi militia.The injured included two Saudi nationals, two Indians, three Nepalese nationals and four Egyptian nationals.In a statement on X, Saudi Civil Defence said emergency response teams had reached the site and initiated necessary procedures to protect lives and property.A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition also confirmed that a tower in the Financial Centre had been targeted, describing the incident as a "cowardly terrorist attack". The spokesperson said authorities were conducting an on-site investigation.Attack amid escalating Saudi-Houthi tensionsThe incident comes amid rising tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi authorities following allegations of Saudi-led coalition airstrikes on telecommunications infrastructure in Yemen's Al-Hudaydah Governorate.In a statement posted on Telegram on Monday, Yemen's Houthi-controlled Ministry of Communications and Information Technology alleged that coalition aircraft had targeted telecommunications buildings, workers' accommodation and a mosque in the governorate.According to the ministry, the strikes killed 17 workers and injured 11 others, based on an initial assessment. articles.title: How Jensen Huang's Silicon Valley friends ran a 'war room' to get him back as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia's chief executive just 11 days after he resigned.
articles.body: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia's chief executive just 11 days after he resigned. The push that got him there started with a small circle of friends in Silicon Valley. Tech founders and investors set up what one of them called a "war room", lobbied Nvidia's board in public and in private, and then pulled in President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, the Financial Times reported.Nvidia's board voted unanimously on November 23 to reinstate Huang. Six days earlier, board chair Harvey Jones had said the company did not intend to bring him back. Huang stepped down on November 12 after reports of two affairs. One was with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. US officials believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The other was with a subordinate.Nvidia shares jumped more than 30% on Monday, the biggest one-day gain in market value on record for a US company, according to The Wall Street Journal.Jensen Huang's allies began lobbying within hours of his resignationAccording to the FT, the group included Uber founder Travis Kalanick, investors Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, and Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood. Within 24 hours, Baker and Gerstner, both large Nvidia shareholders, published an open letter asking the board to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".The effort had Huang's backing, the FT reported. Publicly, Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney threw their weight behind a "Bring Jensen Back" letter. A letter calling for his return gathered more than 200,000 signatures, the WSJ reported, and employees signing it warned of "irreplaceable talent loss".A 45-minute call with JD Vance took Huang's case to the White HouseOne of the allies arranged a 45-minute phone call between Huang and Vance last week. Huang used it to defend his views on US export controls, remote access to chips and his Megaspeed dealings, the FT said.Trump stepped in after returning from China at the end of last week. He asked Vance to talk to Huang and work with the board, The New York Times reported. Vance set out to get the board two things it needed: an assurance that the administration did not see Huang as a national security threat, and a statement that he was not facing criminal charges.The WSJ reported that Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vance on Saturday that Huang was not the target or subject of any Justice Department investigation. Over the next 48 hours, Trump, Vance and other officials relayed that to board members.Trump told the WSJ he reached the board "in numerous ways" and "through representatives", and that the falling stock made his job easier. "The climate became more and more right as the company stock began to tumble," he told the paper. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had earlier called for a leadership shake-up at Nvidia. He softened his stance over the weekend.Nvidia's board took Jensen Huang back after a secret Sunday meetingThe talks were so secretive that interim CEO Colette Kress was kept out, the FT reported. During a long board session on Sunday, Huang disclosed affairs beyond the two already reported and came across as sorry for them, according to the WSJ. After conversations about candour, the board decided his return was the best path.On Monday, Huang walked into Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters to cheering staff. "I'm terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this," he said. At an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, he told employees he was in therapy for 90 minutes a day. He called the idea that Trump pressured the board "completely untrue", the NYT reported.Even after the rally, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago, the FT noted. Nvidia and Huang still face FBI and SEC probes, plus congressional investigations. Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have been summoned to hearings in Washington next week.The board says its internal investigation will continue and that Nvidia will hire a chief compliance officer. On Monday, the US Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: In first all-hands meeting after his return to Nvidia as CEO, Jensen Huang again apologised to employees; and said that the meeting he had with his wife was …
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologised to employees for violating the company’s code of conduct.
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologised to employees for violating the company’s code of conduct. At his first all-hands meeting since returning as CEO, Huang said personal mistakes had hurt his family and led him to resign. He also told the company’s staff that it was the toughest company meeting he had ever held and the second toughest meeting of his life.“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” Huang said, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. He even told employees that he had been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it had “been helping me a lot.” He added, “I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”What Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees about the code of conductHuang said he had written much of Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he said was meant to “create an environment that’s safe for people.” He told employees the company would take violations seriously and weigh the circumstances before deciding how to respond.“That does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said, adding that “facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor into the decision.Huang also rejected suggestions that his standing in Silicon Valley had earned him special treatment. “There are rumours on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” he said.Jensen Huang says he will seek feedback as often as once a monthHuang acknowledged that his management style had sometimes undermined people who worked with him. “It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” he said.“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He told staff he would undergo a 360-degree performance review and could seek feedback from colleagues as often as once a month. He said the review would apply only to him.Huang also pointed to Nvidia’s flexible work policies as he sought to reassure women at the company. “If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” he said.Nvidia’s board is continuing its investigationNvidia announced Huang’s return on Monday, after he stepped down following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia said its board voted unanimously to reinstate him after discussions with Huang and input from senior US government officials.A committee of independent Nvidia directors is still investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week, the report added.Huang told employees his brief absence showed Nvidia could keep running without him. “I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” he said.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal
articles.summary: The deal is said to be the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling a refugee permanently overseas.
articles.body:
The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.

The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini.

The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years.

The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died.

Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.

In 2024, the Labour government scrapped a controversial plan to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda. Now it wants to send failed asylum seekers overseas to third countries when they cannot be sent to their home countries, but is yet to announce any deals. Last week, five EU countries reached a deal to send people whose claims have been refused to Rwanda.

The Eswatini deal raises questions about how much the UK government should disclose about such arrangements, and how it protects both the people it sends overseas and the communities that receive them.

The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public was its priority and that it "continue[s] to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case".

Peramalya's family is demanding answers about his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using their country as a "dumping ground".

In 2021, the Royal Navy rescued Peramalya in the Indian Ocean, along with dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers, as they tried to sail from India to Canada.

They were then detained in a camp on Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory, run exclusively as a UK-US military base.

The island's authorities, who answer to London, recognised that Peramalya and others could not safely return to Sri Lanka, and awarded them refugee protections. But the group remained in the camp for three years while British officials debated their future. A court later ruled their detention had been unlawful.

As a teenager, Peramalya had been tortured and sexually abused by officers in the Sri Lankan military and was later diagnosed with PTSD. During his detention on Diego Garcia, his mental health deteriorated, according to court papers. He suffered from depression and anxiety, and repeatedly attempted suicide. UN inspectors who came to the island raised concerns over the conditions he was being kept in.

While there, he committed a series of crimes, including assault and arson, during two suicide attempts, and spent 24 weeks in prison. He was also convicted of four counts of sexual assault for which he received a suspended prison sentence.

In December 2024, most of the Sri Lankan asylum seekers were allowed to enter the UK but ministers refused to let Peramalya join them because of his crimes. He remained on Diego Garcia.

The High Court upheld the UK's refusal to admit him, in part because of the risk he posed and because ministers were making genuine efforts to find somewhere else safe for him to live. Court documents, seen by the BBC, show the UK approached more than 20 countries and could not secure an agreement.

Then, in February 2026, the US began using its military base on Diego Garcia in its war with Iran. The island authorities began withdrawing non-essential personnel.

At the end of March, the Maldives offered to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was transferred there before being sent on to Eswatini, formerly known as Swaziland.

At the time of his death, the British and Eswatini governments had been finalising the agreement for Peramalya to live there permanently, with the UK to pay for the "reasonable costs" of his accommodation, healthcare, and other support for up to three years.

The document does not specify a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage the risks Peramalya posed to himself and others. But it explicitly acknowledged he required support that would meet his basic needs and protect his physical and mental health, and wellbeing.

Peramalya's family has told the BBC he was initially placed in an isolated guesthouse on his own.

Speaking from India, his sister said the family had not been aware of the plan to make his transfer permanent, and that his mental health had worsened while in the country.

She said he would call her four times a day. "My brother did not want to go there at all," she said. "He couldn't manage being there alone, he was very lonely." The family also said it had been unaware of sexual offences committed by him.

He initially saw a psychiatrist weekly, she said. Later, after his mental health declined, he had daily appointments, and an attendant was brought in to prepare his food.

The UN's refugee agency, which had previously raised concerns about Peramalya's condition on Diego Garcia, said it was "deeply saddened" by his death and stressed that refugees being transferred to other different countries must be protected.

"UNHCR recognises that asylum seekers and refugees may, in certain circumstances, be lawfully transferred to a third country. However, this requires that specific safeguards are in place and those conditions are fulfilled in practice."

Peter Walsh, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, described the case as "highly unusual".

"In most cases, people with criminal convictions who cannot be returned to their home country would simply remain in the UK. Third countries are generally quite reluctant to accept foreign national offenders," he said.

It is unclear how Britain chose Eswatini, but the kingdom had already agreed to accept US deportees under President Trump's wider programme of sending migrants to countries across Africa and Latin America. In 2025, the Trump administration paid Eswatini $5.1m (£3.9m) to accept up to 160 people.

Melusi Simelane, of the Southern African Litigation Centre, who is challenging the US deal in court, said migrant transfers were putting pressure on his country's limited resources.

"Our healthcare system is crumbling, not to mention our mental healthcare, so it is a big ask to bring people into our society who need a lot of support," he said.

"Africa is becoming a dumping ground for the world's unresolved problems."

Zakithi Sibandze, of the Eswatini Rural Women's Assembly, which campaigns to protect women and girls, said it was "very painful" that a sex offender had been relocated to her country.

"Why did they think it was okay to send him to Africa?" she asked. "The UK seems to be saying it is fine for people to commit crimes against women in poor countries."

Earlier this year, the UN's special rapporteur on migrants' rights, Gehad Madi, urged governments to publish the terms of their migration arrangements with other countries and subject them to parliamentary and public oversight. "Strengthening transparency is essential to reduce human rights risks, ensure accountability and uphold the rule of law," he said.

Neither the UK nor Eswatini authorities answered the BBC's questions on the circumstances surrounding Peramalya's resettlement, but a spokesperson for the British government said: "Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high-harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK."

articles.title: Bangladesh garment workers win 36% pay rise after weeks of protest
articles.summary: The protests have cost Bangladesh hundreds of millions, but workers are yet to accept the offer.
articles.body:
Workers in Bangladesh’s garment sector have been offered a 36 percent pay rise after months of protests that are estimated to have cost the country’s economy hundreds of millions of dollars.

The chairman of Bangladesh’s government-appointed garment industry wage board said on Wednesday that the “majority” of the board had agreed to increase the sector’s minimum wage from 12,500 taka ($100) to 17,500 taka ($136) monthly.

Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”. It earns roughly $38bn a year, employs four million people, and accounts for four-fifths of the country’s exports. Many of the industry’s workers are women in rural areas.

The 17,500 taka offered is below the 30,000 taka ($240) that protesters had asked for, and it’s not currently clear whether they will accept the amount offered.

“Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the labour representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters. Akhter urged workers to return to their factories.

“Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.”

The wage hike will take effect in December, with workers receiving the new salaries in January.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated $428m in losses, while orders worth $254m had moved to other countries.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter, behind China. Home to 170 million people, the garment industry has proved an economic success story that has driven development in the South Asian country.

That has, at times, come at a cost: in 2013, the Rana Plaza factory collapse killed 1,134 people and injured thousands, exposing poor safety standards and working conditions for the millions of workers in the industry.

Numerous other incidents, including fires, have resulted in deaths – sometimes killing dozens .

articles.title: An Illinois nursing assistant was allegedly asked to take unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy because she could not lift heavy weights at work; her employer will now pay $160,000 after she filed a pregnancy discrimination lawsuit
articles.summary: Prairie Green at Fay's Point, an assisted living facility in Blue Island, Illinois, will pay $160,000 in lost wages to a former nursing assistant under a
articles.body: Prairie Green at Fay's Point, an assisted living facility in Blue Island, Illinois, will pay $160,000 in lost wages to a former nursing assistant under a federal settlement, the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) announced in a press release on 17 November. The EEOC sued the facility in September 2025 after the company fired a pregnant woman who had developed a pregnancy-related lifting restriction.The pregnant employee couldn’t lift weights, so they fired herAccording to the pregnancy discrimination lawsuit filed by the EEOC, the facility violated the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) when it terminated a certified nursing assistant after she developed a pregnancy-related lifting restriction. The company allegedly told her that lifting weights was an essential part of her job and gave her only one option: to take unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy.Arinnie Young started working at the facility in December 2020 as a certified nursing assistant, according to a Chicago Tribune report. In April 2023, she told the director of nursing that she was pregnant. She also gave the company a doctor's note stating that she could not lift more than 20 pounds or lift residents, according to the EEOC's complaint. For a while, Young avoided lifting residents by swapping them with a co-worker, without making a formal accommodation request, the complaint says.Lifting was essential or go home without payYoung made an official request, but it was denied. Officials told her that unpaid leave for the rest of her pregnancy was her only option, the EEOC said. She refused, and the company dismissed her on 15 August 2023. This conduct violated the PWFA, which requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related restrictions unless doing so would cause an undue hardship for the business. These accommodations may include temporarily excusing an employee from an essential job duty, modifying her responsibilities, offering light-duty work or assigning her to a vacant position. The law also prohibits employers from forcing pregnant employees to take leave when other reasonable accommodations would allow them to continue working.“The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act requires employers to consider reasonable accommodations that allow pregnant employees to remain on the job, including temporary modifications to their duties or reassignment to a vacant position,” EEOC Chair Andrea R. Lucas said.The EEOC also alleged that the facility advertised a concierge position less than a month later, but management never told Young about the opening or offered it to her. She could have performed that work despite her lifting restriction, the agency said.A pregnancy discrimination lawsuitThe EEOC first attempted to resolve the matter through its administrative conciliation process, but the effort failed. The agency then filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, a federal law that requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related restrictions unless doing so would cause an undue hardship.The company must pay Young $160,000 in lost wages. With this settlement, the case ends without a trial. It must also review and revise its pregnancy accommodation policies and establish guidelines for accommodations in jobs that require lifting. Employees will receive annual training on their rights and the employer's obligations under the law.Lucas said the agency would hold employers accountable. “Employers cannot simply force pregnant workers onto unpaid leave when reasonable accommodations are available. This settlement sends a clear message that the EEOC will hold employers accountable for failing to meet their obligations under the PWFA.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe: Arrest warrant issued for Robert Mugabe's son in Zimbabwe
articles.summary: The son of Zimbabwe's late former President Robert Mugabe has faced multiple legal troubles in the recent past.
articles.body:
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.

Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.

In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.

He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.
