articles.title: Sentences served, but Gaza prisoners remain behind Israeli bars
articles.summary: Palestinian families in Gaza wait for loved ones who remain in Israeli prisons despite completing their sentences.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Fadi Zughra’s four children were excited in February when they heard that he’d finally been released from Israeli prison .

He’d been incarcerated since 2016 and completed an 8.5-year sentence in early 2025, but stayed locked up.

So when friends called up to say that Fadi, 43, was at southern Gaza’s Nasser Hospital, his children rushed to get ready to go and greet him.

But his wife, Shmou, hesitated and insisted that they had to verify with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) that he had actually been released.

She was right to double-check. Fadi was still in prison.

“I was shocked, and the girls were very upset. One of my daughters even fainted,” she said.

Fadi is among 48 prisoners from Gaza who remain in Israeli custody after completing their sentences, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs. Their continued detention raises questions about the legal grounds for holding them after their prison terms have expired.

Palestinian prisoners’ organisations say Israel has used its Unlawful Combatants Law to continue detaining Palestinians from Gaza.

Passed in 2002, the law allows the detention of people classified as “unlawful combatants” without a criminal conviction, subject to detention orders and judicial review.

Fadi was arrested on August 15, 2016, while fishing at sea, detained alongside other fishermen. He had worked as a fisherman since childhood.

“The first thing we heard was that he had been killed,” Shmou said. “After about three days, the Red Cross told us he was in prison.”

Fadi had been accused of smuggling and sabotage – allegations Shmou rejected, insisting that he was simply a fisherman trying to earn a living.

For Hanan Harara, the wife of another prisoner, Hisham Harara, the wait has also been marked by repeated hopes of reunion. Whenever news spreads of a prisoner release, she searches the lists for her husband’s name.

On one occasion, after hearing that a group of prisoners had arrived at Gaza’s European Hospital, Hanan and her children rushed there from Deir el-Balah, where they had been displaced. But he did not come home.

Her children have grown tired of the repeated disappointment.

“They tell me, ‘Mum, you keep checking the lists. We don’t want to look at them any more,’” Hanan said. “But I still check. I keep hoping that perhaps this time he will be among those released.”

Hisham completed a nine-year sentence in December 2024, but remains in Israeli custody. His wife said the family had counted down the days while displaced in southern Gaza, as a result of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war.

“But that date [of his release] passed, and we are still waiting,” Hanan said.

Hisham was arrested in December 2015, while travelling through the Beit Hanoon crossing (called Erez in Israel) between Israel and Gaza to reach Jenin in the occupied West Bank, where he worked. He operated heavy machinery and bulldozers, and had previously worked clearing rubble and demolishing buildings damaged during Israel’s 2014 war on Gaza.

Hanan said the allegations against him were related to tunnels, despite his work involving rubble removal and demolition above ground.

These cases come amid a wider rise in the number of Palestinians held in Israeli prisons and detention facilities.

B’Tselem has reported that the Israel Prison Service held 9,187 Palestinians on security grounds at the end of June 2026, including 1,554 from Gaza.

Palestinian prisoners’ institutions reported in October that more than 9,400 Palestinians were in Israeli custody, including 1,419 detainees from Gaza classified by Israel as “unlawful combatants”.

Conditions for Palestinians held in Israeli prisons have deteriorated since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, and the start of Israel’s war on Gaza on the same date.

The United Nations and human rights organisations have documented widespread torture , including beatings, starvation, and rape. The UN Human Rights Office said in September that it had verified the deaths of at least 92 Palestinians in Israeli custody since October 2023.

Children growing up without their fathers

For the families, the separation has become even harder since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began.

Shmou and her children – Almasa and Shahd, both 16, Lana, 14, and Sakher, 11 – used to visit Fadi roughly every two months. Their last visit was about six weeks before the war. Since then, she said, they have not had any news about him.

Sakher was around seven months old when his father was arrested, but grew attached to his father during the prison visits.

“When Sakher visited Fadi, he would tell him, ‘Dad, I want to do this’ and ‘Dad, I want to do that.’ His psychological state has been very difficult,” Shmou said.

Hanan has raised her seven children without Hisham. Their youngest daughter, Eileen, was a baby when he was arrested. She is now 12. Her eldest son, Amjad, was 18 at the time and is now 28.

“When Hisham was detained, I became both a mother and a father,” Hanan said.

Both women have also struggled to learn what their husbands know about the war and whether they are receiving information about their families.

Shmou said former prisoners sometimes pass messages from Fadi, telling her that he is alive and wants to know whether she and the children are safe.

But she worries about reports that detainees are sometimes given false information about the deaths of relatives.

“The Israelis tell him that his family has been killed, or that one of his children has been killed,” she said. “They play with his mental state and his nerves.”

The ICRC has said it has been unable to visit Palestinian detainees in Israeli detention facilities since Israel’s war on Gaza started, limiting its ability to monitor their conditions directly.

During the war, Shmou and her children were displaced from western Gaza City, moving between Khan Younis and Rafah in search of safety.

With Fadi still in prison, she had to shoulder the responsibility of raising their four children and managing daily life alone.

Her brother, Mohammad, became her main source of support, helping her care for the children and deal with the challenges of displacement. But he was killed during the war, about a year and a half ago.

“He was always with me,” Shmou said. “He would stay at my home and take care of things for me.”

Hanan, meanwhile, also had to raise her seven children alone through the war and repeated displacement.

The war added to the responsibilities both women had already been carrying alone. They had to care for their children and find shelter as they were displaced, while not knowing about their husbands’ fate.

Years after their arrests, both women are still calling for their release and waiting for them to return home.

Hanan said the family wants Hisham to know they are still there, waiting for him. “We want him to be reassured that we are OK,” she said. “We want him to know that we are still here.”

Shmou’s wish is for Fadi to return before more of his children’s lives pass without him.

“I want him to be released,” she said. “His daughters have grown up, and his son has grown up too. He is losing his youth.”

articles.title: Is Russia really aiming for a new European security architecture?
articles.summary: Moscow is piling on new demands in talks with Ukraine, either as a negotiating strategy or as a diversion.
articles.body:
How do you stop the Ukraine war after nearly five years of bloodshed and destruction? The administration of United States President Donald Trump seems to believe the path forward is mediation between Moscow and Kyiv.

Earlier this month, it restarted three-way talks with a meeting in Abu Dhabi. But instead of some outline of a deal, what we got was Russia adding yet another item of disagreement by bringing up European security architecture.

To stop pounding Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure, Russia is demanding far-reaching concessions by both the US and Europe. The wish-list includes NATO withdrawing forces from allies on the eastern flank and committing not to accept new members.

At some level, there is nothing new about the Russian demands. In December 2021, weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia presented the US and NATO with two draft treaties which spelled out similar conditions.

The US rejected the far-reaching demands, which included scrapping NATO’s open-door policy, rolling back defence infrastructure and deployments in the east to the levels of 1997, and withdrawing US nuclear arms from Europe. Yet Washington was ready to engage on certain issues, including negotiations on intermediate and short-range missiles stationed in Europe, as well as transparency, risk reduction, and arms control.

Future historians may argue whether the acceptance of the entire package would have averted the war. But Russia’s ambition to recast the European security and political order was already there, in stark display, in late 2021. Ever since, Moscow has stuck to its guns – repeating at every twist and turn that “the root causes” of the conflict have to be addressed in a settlement.

One might agree or disagree about the merits of Russia’s perspective – blaming the war fully on the US and NATO and portraying its own actions as purely defensive. However, there is no denying how radical a cure the Kremlin prescribes to the alleged ills of Western expansion.

One would think that the failure to subdue Ukraine would have injected a dose of realism. A de facto partition of Ukrainian territory, with a ceasefire freezing the front lines, and gradual lifting of Western sanctions, is fully within Putin’s grasp. That is the message he is getting from both Trump and European leaders.

But at least officially, the Kremlin is having none of it. Instead, it is piling up new conditions: the cessation of European military support for Kyiv, no deployment of forces on Ukrainian soil, Finland exiting NATO and reverting to neutrality, prohibition of Ukraine’s participation in the European Union’s budding defence initiatives, no extension of the British and French nuclear umbrella to their European allies, etc.

In other words, nearly all gains Europe has made since February 2022 in terms of strengthening its collective defence have to go in order for Russia to stop fighting. It seems Putin’s ambitions know no bounds.

Obviously, such an overhaul of European security arrangements is, to put it politely, not very likely. Even Trump, however eager he might be to cut a deal with “his friend” Putin, will not be willing, much less able, to deliver Europe on a silver platter.

Ukraine will not stop fighting – it made that abundantly clear with the successful strikes against the Kerch bridge and Russian ships in the Baltic and off Libya’s coast in the Mediterranean. Nor will Europe – for all the uncertainty about funding and the rise of Ukraine-sceptical parties and leaders in key countries – stop supporting Kyiv.

The Russian side is fully aware of the limits and constraints, and yet it hammers on with the same talking points over and over again. The question is why.

The more benign interpretation of Russia’s overly ambitious demands has to do with basic negotiation strategy. Russia is setting a very high asking price in order to extract as much as is realistically possible in the talks with the US and the Europeans.

Once the guns fall silent, there will be practical issues of managing the Cold War-like standoff between NATO and Russia as well as between a Western-backed Ukraine and Russia. Some guardrails would probably be welcomed by both sides on transparency of troop and equipment movements and joint exercises.

There could be military-to-military dialogue or an open line between security and intelligence agencies. It is even possible that there could be some common understandings on hybrid warfare – acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and the like, which have recently been on the rise.

Trying to prevent and/or manage escalation through a new security regime could be possible. The Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), in which both EU member states and Russia participate, could get a new lease of life in such a scenario.

A return to summits involving Russia, on one side, and the US and major European countries on the other might also be a possibility, especially after Putin is gone.

The more sceptical interpretation of Russia’s demands is that it is trying to dilute the agenda and in effect divert attention away from Ukraine in order to gain extra advantage on the battlefield.

In Moscow’s thinking, strategic-level relations between great powers have priority over regional issues. Vladimir Medinsky, Putin’s aide and chief negotiator, put it bluntly: “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and in the Ukraine, there was just a cyst that burst.”

The same logic informed the much-hyped summit in Shenzhen between Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Russian leader basked in his top-dog status in global geopolitics, with nuclear stability and the global price of energy on the agenda.

The US is prepared to indulge Putin. This in turn gives Russia sufficient political licence to shower ballistic missiles and drones on Ukraine through another winter, aiming for a victor’s peace rubber-stamped by the Americans and swallowed as a fait accompli by Europe.

The fact that the Europeans are still not at the diplomatic table – partly because of internal squabbling but also because of Russia’s reluctance to have them included – is telling. Thus, the talk about repairing European security architecture may be little more than another fig leaf for the Russians.

If that is the case, it would be a shame. At the end of the day, avoiding war in Europe should be a goal that all actors – the US, the Europeans, Ukraine, and Russia itself – should be converging on. It may not be the rethink of the continent’s security architecture Moscow has been appealing for but a meaningful contribution to security, nonetheless.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Solomon Islands signs treaty with Australia that checks China’s influence in the South Pacific
articles.summary: The Solomon Islands rejected a secretive 4-year-old defense deal with China that raised fears of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific country and declared Wednesday while signing a treaty with Australia that it would never allow a foreign military base on its soil.
articles.body: The Solomon Islands rejected a secretive 4-year-old defense deal with China that raised fears of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific country and declared Wednesday while signing a treaty with Australia that it would never allow a foreign military base on its soil. The Solomons’ archipelago is sprawled across the sea route between the United States and Australia, from where U.S. Gen. Douglas MacArthur commanded the Pacific campaign in World War II. U.S. allies fought pivotal battles against Japanese forces on the islands during the war, and the country that today has a population of fewer than 900,000 people remains strategically imperative territory in the U.S. struggle against China for global influence. The islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale and his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese signed the bilateral security pact following reports that the Solomons will end its defense treaty with China next year. The new treaty confirms Australia’s place as the Solomons’ “primary security partner” and states “there will be no foreign military or security base” on the smaller nation 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) northeast of Australia, both prime ministers said in a statement. The deal is the latest bilateral security pact Australia has struck with Pacific neighbors since Beijing inked a treaty with the Solomons’ previous government in 2022 that created fears the Chinese navy would build a base in the South Pacific. Since Albanese’s government was first elected in late 2022, Australia, a staunch U.S. ally, has been attempting to edge Chinese influence out of the region through bilateral security agreements with countries including Fiji, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. Australia reached a security-linked pact with Papua New Guinea in 2024 that promised Australia’s nearest neighbor 600 million Australian dollars ($396 million) over a decade to include a rugby league team in the Australian national competition. Wale would not confirm or deny news media reports that his government had told Beijing that the security pact with China, which has provided Chinese police trainers to the Solomons’ capital Honiara, would not be renewed when it expires after five years in early 2027. “Unfortunately there is a non-disclosure clause in the treaty with China,” Wale told reporters in a press conference with Albanese at Australian Parliament House. “So I am unable to talk about that. We have ongoing discussions with China.” “As you know, Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done. Gone. We don’t want to be there again,” he added. In Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not directly answer a journalist’s question about whether the Solomons had said it would end the Chinese security pact. “China always follows the principle of mutual respect and equality in developing relations with the Solomon Islands,” Guo said Tuesday. “There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands.” Albanese said the new bilateral treaty elevated bilateral relations to a “level which has never been seen before and has never been stronger.” The treaty is broader than security. Australia has agreed to also invest in Solomons’ infrastructure, education, renewable energy and sport. Oliver Nobetau, Pacific Islands program director at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney think tank, described the treaty as significant and fine-tuned to the Solomons’ priorities. “It demonstrates that Australia is listening to what the Pacific partners want,” Nobetau told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

articles.title: Rising prices push families to the brink in Yemen’s Hodeidah
articles.summary: Renewed fighting, rising fuel costs and shrinking incomes deepen the struggle to survive in the Houthi-controlled city.
articles.body:
Hodeidah, Yemen – Standing beside his rented motorcycle taxi near the Othman market in central Hodeidah, Ahmed Arjash starts each day early in the morning looking for passengers, hoping to earn enough to feed his family of six.

In his late 30s, Arjash also delivers small goods for merchants. By evening, he needs to have made enough money to buy flour, rice and bread, and for the day’s rent on the motorcycle. He falls short.

“Before, I would come home with enough food for my family for the day, and maybe save a little to repair the motorcycle or buy medicine if one of my children fell ill,” he told Al Jazeera. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle. Sometimes I go home empty-handed, or with a small bag of food that does nothing for our hunger.”

Across Hodeidah, where the Red Sea port handles the bulk of commercial and humanitarian imports into Yemen’s Houthi-controlled northwest, families are struggling to afford basic goods as renewed fighting compounds the damage of more than a decade of war.

Fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia intensified in July after four years of relative calm, and the Houthis have since made significant advances in Yemen’s southern Red Sea coast region.

Hodeidah port has come under attack by the Saudi-led coalition, but continues to remain open.

In a market in Hodeidah’s al-Salkhana neighbourhood, Umm Sami, a widow raising four children, sells small household goods and takes occasional domestic work. Rising prices have changed how she shops.

“We buy in very small quantities. Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera. “Even bread has become a burden. My children ask for foods they used to eat easily before the war, and I have to stay silent or distract them by talking about something else.”

Across Houthi-controlled areas, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent more in September than in August, its highest price in a year, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report. Food was still available in markets the monitors could reach, but families had less money to spend.

Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to the World Food Programme (WFP).

In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, families are skipping meals or going without meat, fish, milk and fruit. Families without clean water at home must buy it at high prices, and deteriorating health facilities leave many unable to afford treatment.

Public sector employees whose salaries have stopped entirely or in part, and families whose fixed incomes have been eroded by inflation, are also in need. In May, the World Bank said Yemen’s economy contracted by 1.5 percent in 2025 and projected a further 0.5 percent contraction in 2026.

Fishing, long a mainstay of Hodeidah’s economy, has become a losing trade for some.

“The cost of going out to sea, fishing equipment and fuel has risen a lot, while sales and people’s purchasing power in the city keep fluctuating,” said Salem, a fisherman in his 30s. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to. Sometimes a fisherman comes back with barely enough to cover the cost of his trip, if he is lucky.”

Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said days can pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said. “Everything has gone up: food, transport, even the simplest household needs, while income stays the same or shrinks.”

Economic analysts say transport, shipping and fuel costs pass directly to consumers , and that risks to regional shipping have raised insurance and freight costs on imports. Weak demand then shrinks the work available to day labourers.

Fighting earlier this year in Hodeidah governorate’s Hays and al-Khokha districts and elsewhere on the Red Sea coast has forced more families from their homes.

On October 2, the WFP said the fighting had cut off its access to about 350,000 people in parts of Taiz governorate and Hodeidah.

The agency said it had reallocated resources from food distributions scheduled for November to sustain its emergency response, and warned of assistance gaps without new funding. Its monitoring in areas it could reach found 74 percent of households unable to meet their basic food needs.

The WFP suspended its activities in areas under the control of the Houthis in September 2025, after the group detained UN staff members.

For Arjash, the war shows in the dwindling number of passengers who can pay to ride his motorcycle.

“People here walk long distances to save on the fare, and anyone who rides my motorcycle taxi haggles over every rial because their pockets are empty,” he said.

“As you can see, I feel helpless in front of my children when they ask for something simple and I cannot provide it.”

images.caption: Children pass time at al-Wara camp for internally displaced people in al-Khokha of Hodeidah province, Yemen [File: Fawaz Salman/Reuters]

articles.title: Invasive Burmese pythons push farther north into Florida as hunters race to stop ecological devastation
articles.summary: Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years, and now, experts warn they've been spotted further north.
articles.body: Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years. Now, experts warn they are making their way farther north. Hard freezes were once thought to limit Burmese pythons to South Florida, but researchers have documented the invasive snakes sheltering and sometimes breeding in burrows, which can protect them from cold temperatures. "First of all, they're following the food," said Amy Siewe, professional python hunter and guide. "But they are also stealing gopher, tortoise burrows and armadillo burrows. And that's how they're staying warm during those colder nights in Florida that they typically wouldn't be able to survive." For Siewe, python hunting is a full-time job. Known as the "Python Huntress," she left behind a 13-year real estate career in 2019 after discovering Florida's Burmese python problem, turning her lifelong passion for snakes and reptiles into a new purpose. BEAR SWIPES HUNTER'S DEER BEFORE HE GETS A CHANCE TO CLIMB OUT OF HIS TREE STAND TO RETRIEVE IT "They eat 98% of the mammals in parts of the Everglades," said Siewe. "So they're really devastating our ecosystem. So we need to do everything we can to get them out of our ecosystem to save the native wildlife. But also, you know, we don't even know what type of damage this is going to do to our ecosystem in the years to come." Siewe's husband, Dave, and her puppy, Dixie, like to get in on the action, too. Fox News Multimedia Reporter Amy Galo joined them on a hunt through the Everglades in Collier County, getting a firsthand look at what it takes to find the invasive snakes. "She's (Dixie's) really just telling us where they are. And when she finds one, she says her indication," said Siewe as Dixie searched through the brush. "So then I go in. Well, once she sits, Dave calls her off, and I go verify that there's a python." Siewe searches for pythons in the Everglades several times a week, even leading guided hunts. "We've got our snake deck here," said Siewe. "It's a platform on the truck that just gives us a little bit of height so we can see the pythons easier in the grass and in the water and things like that." Conservative estimates place the population of Burmese pythons in the Greater Everglades region in the tens of thousands. An exact count is difficult because these snakes are masters of camouflage. According to Siewe, they spend roughly 85% of their time lying still in often inaccessible areas. "We are always happy catching one, like I always want to catch one more," said Siewe. "There are a lot of times we go out and you don't catch any. That's just the nature of the python." AGGRESSIVE TURKEYS ARE HARASSING PEOPLE ACROSS THE BOSTON AREA JUST DAYS BEFORE THANKSGIVING More than 23,000 Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. But recently, the snakes have also been spotted farther north. "There are two different populations. One in Brevard and also up in Charlotte County," said Siewe. "But based on what we know, the scientists think that those are separate events. So that is not an extension of the colony down here (in the Everglades) that has been established for years." Once a breeding population becomes established, eradication is extremely difficult. "The problem with the pythons is that you don't even know that they're there until it's way beyond your control," explained Siewe. "These guys spend 85% of their time not moving. And so, when we find one python, there could be up to a thousand more that we're not seeing." Siewe added, "They lay eggs, you know, 20 to 40 eggs a year. Sometimes the big ones can lay over 100. So it's just, it's a never-ending cycle." CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP That is why researchers emphasize early detection and public education to try to prevent additional releases of captive invasive snakes.

articles.title: Two Libyan soldiers die after Ukraine attack on Russian vessel
articles.summary: Khalifa Haftar’s Libyan National Army, which Russia backs, vowed retaliation for the death of its soldiers
articles.body:
Two naval officers of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) have died from wounds sustained in a drone attack claimed by Ukraine on a Russian warship near Benghazi port , according to Libya’s eastern-based forces.

The LNA identified the two as Al-Taher Abdullah al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Mohammed al-Said, saying they were wounded in the attack on Sunday night and subsequent explosions on board the targeted vessel, and died on Tuesday.

The LNA’s General Command pledged to retaliate at a time and place of its choosing, saying it would continue to defend Libya’s sovereignty and security.

Libya is divided between a United Nations-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a parallel administration based in the eastern city of Benghazi, backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar. Haftar’s camp has maintained close military and strategic ties with Russia for several years.

Following the attack, his son Saddam Haftar, who is widely seen as heir apparent, said, “It is with deep sadness and great pride that I pay tribute today to two heroes of our naval forces.”

“[They] were martyred as a result of their injuries sustained during the performance of their national duty following the criminal attack on the Benghazi Naval Base,” he wrote on Facebook.

In a separate statement, Oussama Hamad, who heads the eastern government, offered his condolences to the officers. He specified that the two men had died “as a result of their injuries during the treacherous Ukrainian aggression against the port of Benghazi”.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Monday that Kyiv was behind the operation, as seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used to sink the Russian naval corvette on Sunday, leaving 10 people injured. A separate attack targeted a cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi later that day.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Wednesday that Ukraine had been exercising its “absolute right to self-defence” by attacking the Russian ships in Libyan waters.

“Let’s put ourselves in their place. What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy – an invader? Well, we would defend ourselves and, in a sense, exercise our absolute right to self-defence. That is what the Ukrainians are doing,” Barrot told French public broadcaster TF1.

Meanwhile, Libya’s eastern-based government filed a complaint with the UN General Assembly and the Security Council seeking an international investigation into the attacks.

The Tripoli-based internationally recognised Government of National Unity also condemned the attacks. It demanded an explanation from Ukraine, rejecting the use of Libyan territory and waters for foreign military operations , amid fears that Libya might represent a new front in the Russia-Ukraine war.

articles.title: America’s first Thanksgiving was made possible by daring Revolutionary snipers
articles.summary: George Washington delayed the Continental Army's march to Valley Forge as the American Revolutionary War's first national Thanksgiving was proclaimed.
articles.body: By late 1777, the American Revolutionary War looked grim. The British had captured Philadelphia, forcing the Continental Congress to flee to York, Pennsylvania. Gen. George Washington’s main army suffered defeats at Brandywine, Paoli and Germantown and was preparing for a hard winter at Valley Forge. The American victory at the Battle of Saratoga marked a turning point in history and provided much-needed good news that lifted the spirits of the young United States. Revolutionary snipers, led by Col. Daniel Morgan, would be the "Corps the [British] feared the most" in the battles for Saratoga, according to Maj. Gen. Horatio Gates. At the Battle of Freeman’s Farm on Sept. 19, they killed numerous British officers with their "widowmakers," Pennsylvania long rifles. Before and after the battle, they acted as special forces in the no-man’s-land between the two armies, eliminating British scouts who served as their enemies’ eyes and ears, effectively blinding Crown forces. THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER The riflemen’s expert marksmanship proved decisive in the final battle, taking out numerous British officers, including a shot, likely fired by Pvt. Timothy Murphy, that killed British Brig. Gen. Simon Fraser. They also assaulted the British right flank, broke it and stormed several key redoubts, leading to the collapse of the British lines at the Battle of Bemis Heights. The full story of the remarkable Revolutionary snipers and the role of the Pennsylvania Long Rifle in helping win the Revolutionary War can be found in my newest bestselling book, "Revolutionary Snipers: Washington’s Frontier Commandos Whose Marksmanship Forged a New Way of War and Helped Win the Revolution," the third book in a trilogy on the elite units of the war. This groundbreaking look at the Revolutionary War recounts the untold story of the Continental Army’s first soldiers in an immersive "Band of Brothers"-style narrative that puts the reader in the boots of these expert woodsmen, longhunters and scouts — snipers who preceded today’s U.S. Army special operators. THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION At Saratoga, the Americans captured an entire British field army, a first in the war, an event that led to an alliance with France. In response to American success on the battlefield, Congress, meeting in York, appointed a committee that included Sam Adams, Richard Henry Lee and Daniel Roberdeau. On Nov. 1, Congress adopted its recommendation that Dec. 18 be a national day of "solemn Thanksgiving and praise." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION All 13 states observed this first nationwide proclamation of Thanksgiving. Gen. George Washington ordered the Continental Army to delay its move to Valley Forge by one day and observe the occasion with chaplain-led services. One soldier, Joseph Plumb Martin, recalled tongue-in-cheek the "sumptuous" extra Thanksgiving rations given to the starving soldiers: half a gill of rice and a tablespoon of vinegar before the Thanksgiving service. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP States and other communities had previously declared days of Thanksgiving and fasting, but 1777 marked the first National Day of Thanksgiving for the United States of America. The Second Continental Congress proclaimed it for the whole country, as its author Samuel Adams said, "That with one heart and one voice the good people may express the grateful feelings of their hearts." articles.title: If you want to know the dangers of socialism, take a look at Mamdani’s New York
articles.summary: New York City, not Cuba or Venezuela, is America's socialist test as Zohran Mamdani's Rikers Island plan offers 4,500 beds for a 6,600 jail population.
articles.body: Friends, if you want to know what America’s future under socialism might look like, you don’t need to look to Cuba, Venezuela or the failing capitals of Western Europe. Just take the subway in New York City. Under Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani, New York has become the proving ground for America’s latest flirtation with socialism. And we’re already seeing what happens when ideological fantasies collide with reality. RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY The early results aren’t encouraging. Particularly when it comes to public safety. In just the past week, Mamdani has announced two sweeping changes: the dismantling of the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG) and a plan to close Rikers Island and replace it with dramatically fewer jail beds. MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE The impact won’t be immediate (Mamdani conveniently pushed the Rikers plan to 2032). But the implications are enormous — as they will be if the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) brings this agenda to your town. Some background: The SRG was created in 2015 as a specialized police unit responding to major emergencies, violent demonstrations and civil disorder. Anyone who witnessed the 2020 George Floyd riots understands why. Protests deteriorated into widespread looting, assaults and destruction. Think of the 2020 Summer of Love as the DSA’s origin story. MICHAEL RUIZ: NEW YORK'S GUTTED POLICE UNIT WAS MORE THAN A PROTEST SQUAD Yet despite the SRG responding to only about 6% of NYC protests, Mamdani has eliminated it, replacing its protest-management responsibilities with an alphabet soup of units, including something called the "Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division." Yes, really. A civilian-led operation without weapons or arrest powers. MICHAEL RUIZ: RESURFACED VIDEO APPEARS TO SHOW NYC MAYOR ARRESTED BY NYPD GROUP HE IS DISBANDING And if that sounds like Mamdani — arrested at least twice by the SRG himself — is simply handing out jobs to his fellow travelers … he is. Now, the roughly 500 SRG officers will be reassigned and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch insists public safety won’t suffer. MAMDANI’S PLAN TO DISMANTLE NYPD’S RIOT UNIT RIPPED AS ‘SMOKE AND MIRRORS’ BY FORMER FORCE LEADERS Well … we’ll see. Mamdani seems to believe recruiting fellow activists into an "engagement" unit will keep protesters in line. But given that activist groups derive significant status from fighting the police and revenue from suing them … color us skeptical. Then there’s Rikers Island. Mamdani plans to shutter the notorious jail complex by 2032, replacing it with four smaller borough facilities. HOCHUL SILENT ABOUT WOMEN UNDER ATTACK IN AMERICA'S LARGEST CITY AS DEM CANDIDATE STEERS OUTRAGE ELSEWHERE Nobody disputes Rikers has serious problems. But the solution to a badly managed jail isn’t eliminating thousands of beds — especially when thousands still need incarceration. By the numbers, New York’s jail population is approximately 6,600. The replacement system will only accommodate 4,160 inmates, plus 340 specialized therapeutic beds. That’s 4,500 total. Yet despite the SRG responding to only about 6% of NYC protests, Mamdani has eliminated it, replacing its protest-management responsibilities with an alphabet soup of units, including something called the "Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division." So do the math. The city must somehow reduce its jail population by more than 2,000. By roughly one-third. And all this comes as New York has largely abandoned quality-of-life enforcement. The broken-windows philosophy that rescued the city from its crime-ridden past has been discarded over tortured theories of "institutional bias." Fare evasion, aggressive disorderly conduct, public drug use and shoplifting are barely enforced against. Cops are cowed from proactive policing. So, essentially, we don’t lock up many people here as it is. We’re now going to go down by a third? NYC PARENTS AND LOCALS PROTEST HOMELESS MEN'S SHELTER BEING BUILT A SHORT WALK FROM MIDDLE SCHOOL The administration’s answer to this is to promise faster court proceedings, diversion programs, and alternatives to detention. More nonsense. That canard has been floated before. It never works. It’s never really attempted. So, the question remains: What happens if the jail population doesn’t fall as promised? Where do those without jail beds go? Into our neighborhoods. Onto our streets. And inevitably, into New York’s subway system. And it gets better. According to a New York Post report, Mamdani also wants to expand a program paying families $500 monthly to house relatives returning from jail. The program would grow from 50 to 300 families, eventually costing $7.1 million annually. Sensing another blue-city money pit? New York proposes spending billions constructing smaller jails, millions housing former inmates and hundreds of millions on additional services — all while reducing incarceration capacity. The replacement jails alone are expected to cost at least $16 billion — twice the original estimate (New York has a cost overrun? Shocker!). Meanwhile, taxes rise steadily to subsidize this madness. Now, understand: the victims of all this won’t be wealthy progressives living behind doormen or city commissioners with protection details. They’re working-class New Yorkers dependent on public transportation, living in vulnerable neighborhoods, unable to move somewhere safer. And disproportionately: women. So, friends … all this can be yours when socialism comes to town! Because while socialism promises compassion, government services, redistribution and attention to the supposedly "oppressed," it’s politicians like Mamdani — who has never held a real job — deciding where your money goes. And their lack of practical experience and obsession with giveaways is limitless. Is it any wonder that New York State already leads the nation in population loss by percentage? Only California loses more people in raw numbers. None of that seems to matter to our enlightened leaders. Friends, New York isn’t some isolated political curiosity. It’s America’s largest city, still its financial capital, and an enormously influential political center. Policies pioneered here migrate elsewhere. According to a New York Post report, Mamdani also wants to expand a program paying families $500 monthly to house relatives returning from jail. The program would grow from 50 to 300 families, eventually costing $7.1 million annually. So, consider this a heads-up. Watch NYC closely. Mamdani’s DSA experiment will likely be measured in frightened commuters, deteriorating neighborhoods, departing businesses and victims who discover government sympathy for offenders exceeds its concern for everyone else. Because when government stops enforcing the rules, the streets eventually make their own. articles.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade 2026: How to watch, who’s performing, what’s new and more
articles.summary: Learn more about the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, including when to tune in, how to watch it, this year’s performers, who’s hosting and more.
articles.body: It’s a big year for one of American television’s biggest entertainment spectacles as the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade celebrates 100 years of kicking off the holiday season. But a serious rainstorm and strong wind gusts expected to hit New York City on Thursday could hamper the parade. The event’s trademark balloons are still on the roster but could be grounded under New York City regulations that state they can’t fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph. If they’re held down, it would be the first time since 1971. “Our team is closely monitoring the weather forecast with our City and agency partners, and as always, the safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority,” Macy’s said in a statement. The storm will spool up rapidly and is expected to hit Thursday afternoon but possibly during the late morning, federal forecasters said. It could bring as much as 3 inches of rain to parts of the region while pushing wind gusts to a potential 70 mph and soaking areas already expected to see “widespread moderate coastal flooding” from unusually high tides, the National Weather Service said. The parade has marched through rough weather and much more in its previous 99 editions. The event started as Macy’s Christmas Parade in New York City during the Roaring ‘20s before morphing into the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Because the nation’s World War II years demanded all hands on deck, the parade went dark from 1942-44, which is why the parade’s centennial is celebrated at this year’s event, according to Macy’s. Macy’s says the celebration will meet the occasion, with major parade elements and marquee entertainment planned, and Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker of NBC’s “TODAY” show reprising their roles as hosts of the television broadcast. A parade for history The first parade was the brainchild of Macy’s employees, who wanted to celebrate the upcoming holidays and bring attention to what was the world’s largest department store, according to Macy’s. It took place on Nov. 27, 1924, with tigers and other zoo animals on hand, a jazz band and a few other musical acts, and a man performing as Santa Claus. An estimated 250,000 people took it all in, according to New York state’s Division of Tourism. Trademark elements such as massive balloons joined in 1927 with the addition of cartoon character Felix the Cat and the subtraction of big cats and other zoo animals. Helium took the balloons higher in 1928, sparking a tradition of letting them loose at the end of the event and offering rewards and cash prizes for their return to Macy’s. In 1932, pilot Annette Gibson, 22, allegedly directed her plane to crash into a wayward parade balloon, causing the aircraft to plummet in a tailspin that was only thwarted at the last minute, according to The New York Times’ coverage of the incident. The next year, Macy’s announced it was ending the release-and-catch promotion. In 1947, the comedy and drama “Miracle on 34th Street” followed the world of a Macy’s Santa Claus. It cemented the parade as a cultural cornerstone and paved the way for NBC to air it nationally in 1953, making it a coast-to-coast tradition and the most-watched entertainment telecast of the year, according to NBC. The parade route today is not the Harlem-to-Midtown, 6-mile workout it was in 1924. It’s been slashed to 2.5 miles. When and where Assuming the parade goes off as previously planned, it will take its first steps at 8:30 a.m. Thursday on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City. It usually wraps up by noon. Where’s the parade headed? It generally marches from the Upper West Side to Midtown and Macy’s Herald Square flagship store on 34th Street — a 2.5-mile trek. A New York City Department of Transportation map shows the route will take floats, balloons, marchers and other participants down Central Park West before heading east on West 59th Street and south again on 6th Avenue before reaching 34th Street. How to watch from home or in person The parade will be broadcast and streamed at 8:30 a.m. Thursday in all time zones on NBC and Peacock, with an encore scheduled for 2 p.m. on NBC, and will air live on Telemundo, according to the network. In-person viewing will be available along designated portions of the route. More to watch If you’re a Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade superfan, this just might be your year. The day before the big event, the “Countdown to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” special will broadcast live from the parade’s starting line, according to NBC. It will air and stream Wednesday from 8 p.m. to 9 p.m. on NBC and Peacock. Comedian Jack McBrayer, known for his portrayal of Kenneth Parcell on “30 Rock,” will host as viewers get a first look at some of the floats and balloons and the stories behind them, according to the network. The special will also feature appearances by actress and singer Mckenna Grace and Grammy Award and Tony Award winner Leslie Odom Jr. What’s special this year? Performers from nine iconic Broadway shows will participate in a 10-minute medley outside Macy’s, according to the department store and NBC. The “musical journey” will celebrate elements of “The Book of Mormon,” “Chicago,” Disney’s “Aladdin,” “Hamilton,” “The Lost Boys,” “Rent,” Richard O’Brien’s “The Rocky Horror Show,” “Schmigadoon!” and “Wicked,” according to NBC. Macy’s also said it will present the parade’s largest-ever number of balloons and “inflatable elements” — 100 in all — for the occasion. They’ll include a selection of Macy’s Blue Sky Gallery balloons from iconic artists and creatives such as Tim Burton, Keith Haring, Jeff Koons and Yayoi Kusama, according to NBC. New floats will include Dashing All the Way with DoorDash, Hogwarts Holiday with HBO, Mr. Peanut Power Plant with Planters, Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs, Road Trip to Parade with Geico, and Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes by Macy’s, according to the network. Macy’s All-Star floats will include stars of parades past, including Angry Birds’ Red, Arthur, Bugs Bunny, Bullwinkle J. Moose, Curious George, Adventure Time’s Finn & Jake, Jimmy Neutron, Popeye & Olive Oyl & Swee’Pea, Pink Panther, Poppy from “Trolls,” Scooby-Doo, Sonic the Hedgehog, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and Wild Thing, NBC said. New character floats include depictions of Bluey by BBC, Buckaroo Bob the Minion by Illumination, Earl the Squirrel by Universal Orlando Resort, Hello Kitty Big Apple by Sanrio, Joe Cool & Woodstock by Peanuts Worldwide, Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey by Disney, Underdog by DreamWorks Animation, and a new balloonicle (a balloon with a vehicle inside that is driven down the route), Fuzzyeti’s Fur Wheel Drive by Levi’s, according to the network. Macy’s said the parade will also honor Fiona the hippo, who died last week following complications from eating a hat that landed in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo. The department store said in an Instagram Stories post that it “wanted to mark Fiona’s memory” as a beloved hippo who captured the hearts of zoo visitors after she was born premature in 2017. Macy’s said it has made a donation to the zoo and, during the return of the parade’s circa-1931 Blue Hippopotamus balloon, handlers on the ground will wear a purple Fiona patch. Who’s performing? Organizers have put together big names fit for a festival: Country music’s Megan Moroney and Grammy Award-nominated artist Teddy Swims will headline the Herald Square stage. Performance and dance groups will dazzle paradegoers, and marching bands from schools across the country will keep the beat going down the route. Floats along the route will carry Baha Men, Natasha Bedingfield, Blues Traveler, Devo, Feid, Mckenna Grace, Icona Pop, Il Volo, Indigo Girls, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Ejae, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Natalie Merchant, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Keke Palmer, Anthony Ramos, RIIZE and Smash Mouth, with numerous special appearances planned and additional performances to be added to the lineup, NBC said. NBCUniversal is the parent company of NBC, NBC News, Peacock, Telemundo, Illumination, Universal Orlando Resort, and DreamWorks Animation.

articles.title: 2 men charged with burglary after break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate’s country home
articles.summary: Two men have been charged in connection with a burglary at the Sandringham estate, police said, after a reported break-in at the home of Prince William and Kate.
articles.body: LONDON — Two men have been charged in connection with a burglary at the royal family’s Sandringham estate, British police said Wednesday, after a reported break-in at the country home of Prince William and Princess Kate. The pair were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site, the local police force said in a statement. Officers were called just before 6 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET) on Monday “to reports of suspicious activity at a property,” Norfolk Police force said. “Police and specialist resources attended and two men were arrested nearby on suspicion of burglary and trespass and taken into custody for questioning,” the statement added. The two men, named by police as Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, have now been charged. They remain in custody and are due to appear in court in the eastern city of Norwich on Wednesday morning, the statement said. The Sun newspaper first reported Tuesday that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, one of the residences used by the heir to the British throne and his wife. The property, gifted to the couple by the late Queen Elizabeth II as a wedding present, is nestled in the heart of the royals’ sprawling estate. In an earlier statement, police said the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident. Separately, a royal source told NBC News that the couple and their three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, were not there at the time. The couple and their children have often enjoyed weekend breaks and holidays at the royal estate in eastern England. Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom country house built in the early 1800s, entered the royals’ extensive property portfolio when it was bought in 1898 by Queen Victoria’s son, who would later become King Edward VII. The prince and princess of Wales’ main home is Forest Lodge in Windsor, a small town around 30 miles west of London. The couple said they moved there for a “fresh start” in 2025 after the death of the late queen and Kate’s cancer diagnosis. The break in came days before the release of a new documentary about Kate’s cancer diagnosis and remission, called “Heal.” Set to air on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on Peacock from Dec. 1., the highly personal film will see her share her private thoughts on her illness and recovery. “It changes your body, it changes you physically, but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you,” Kate says in a clip released ahead of Sunday’s air date “It is often through pain that we realize there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that,” she adds.

articles.title: ‘We need to be seen’: Over a third of UK Muslim students face Islamophobia
articles.summary: From being spat on and assaulted to suffering humiliation, Muslims on campus are increasingly vulnerable, report says.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Haanyah Cassam, 23, was only a few weeks into her first year at the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) when a security guard walked into a hall where she and other students had gathered for a lecture.

According to Cassam, the guard told them they were behaving “like a pack of animals, especially those hijabis”. He then made a remark about “towel heads” and walked off.

Cassam, who chose to wear the hijab despite her family’s fears for her safety, told Al Jazeera, “It takes a lot of confidence and a lot of power to put something on your head that you know is going to make you a target.”

At the time, she felt “there was no one we could go to about this”, she said.

She later raised the issue with a professor, and was told their hands were tied by bureaucracy. The guard left the university at the end of that year.

Cassam, who studied global liberal arts and is now training as an English teacher at University College London (UCL), said that on another occasion, someone spat at her as she entered university.

Cassam’s experience reflects the findings of a report released on Wednesday by the Federation of Student Islamic Societies (FOSIS), which found that 38 percent of Muslim students in the United Kingdom have experienced Islamophobia at university.

The survey carried out this year of 715 students at 63 universities found women were more likely to be targeted than men, at 42 percent compared with 34 percent. The rate was highest at Russell Group universities, the UK’s leading research institutions, where 53 percent of Muslim women reported Islamophobia.

Back in 2005, about 25 percent said they experienced Islamophobia.

For Cassam, being spat on hurt less than what she heard in lectures.

She recalled a lecturer who, while teaching Mauritanian poetry and dance, told the class that Islam forbade Muslim women from expressing themselves artistically, calling it “savage” and “uncivilised”. When Cassam objected, she was told: “You’re just one Muslim.”

Her dissertation examined the emotional impact of Prevent, the UK government’s “counterterrorism” programme, on Muslim students. She said the academic meant to oversee it refused to help and told her she would not give it a mark of more than 50.

She did not take the matter further. “I was told it’s best not to rock the boat,” Cassam said. She found another tutor to supervise her, and was awarded a first-class honours mark of 76.

Wednesday’s survey painted a grim picture of abuse. In one example, a group of students had urine thrown at them while wearing the hijab, which the university in question would not classify as a hate crime.

Another student said that when they tried to report an incident, they were told to go home if they did not like being in the UK.

A separate student said they were locked out of a lab session after asking to attend Friday prayers.

Of those affected, 68 percent did not feel able to report it, and almost half of all respondents did not know how. Of those who did report, 45 percent felt their concerns were not dealt with properly.

Islamophobia on campus also had an effect on mental health, with 45 percent reporting a moderate to high impact.

Three in five said they felt afraid or intimidated to express their views on Palestine.

FOSIS is calling on universities and students’ unions to adopt a definition of Islamophobia, train staff and student leaders, and give it a category in reporting systems, with complaints against staff investigated outside the staff member’s department. It also wants Friday prayers protected in timetables, no exams on Eid, and the government to review Prevent.

“Too often [students] stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable,” said Rahma Hegy, FOSIS vice president for student affairs. “That lack of accountability concerns us most.”

At the University of York, Aayan Hashmi, 20, a second-year law student and president of the Islamic Society, said his faculty and the students’ union were supportive.

Sports and social societies centre on pub crawls and bar crawls, and Muslim students who do not drink “could be the best player” and still never fully realise their potential, he said.

Last year, as he walked to his first-year house after Friday prayers, a driver rolled down his window and gave him the middle finger.

Students have also told him they feel forced “to choose between their faith and their studies” when Friday prayers clash with lectures.

The FOSIS survey found that 21 percent of students said their timetable was “not compatible at all” with daily and Friday prayers.

Muslim students at the university are currently pressing the university for a larger prayer space.

At the University of Cambridge, Syed Ali, 21, a final-year politics and international relations student, said that rather than slurs, prejudice is dressed in “academic” and “sophisticated” language to make it appear legitimate.

Ali said it can be hard to tell where racism ends and Islamophobia begins.

“It’s difficult to disentangle,” he said.

The FOSIS report found that half of respondents counted the racialisation of Muslims as Islamophobia. Several described racial slurs in a survey about religious hatred, and the report says Muslims’ faith and race are “often read together”.

“It has been a very frightening experience to start realising that the world does not love me as I love it,” Cassam said. She is now urging others to speak out.

“We need people to report,” she said. “Statistics are political, and we need to be seen in policy.”

Al Jazeera contacted SOAS, the University of York and the University of Cambridge for responses, but did not receive replies by the time of publication.

articles.title: 6 people dead, including 2 children, after plane crashes off Mississippi coast
articles.summary: Two boys, ages 8 and 10, were among those killed when a Cessna 210 aircraft lost contact with air traffic control on Tuesday afternoon.
articles.body:
Six people, including two children, were killed Tuesday when a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

The Coast Guard said it had found the remains of all six individuals aboard a downed Cessna 210 aircraft approximately 2 miles northeast of Horn Island, Mississippi.

Officials said the plane descended at 10,000 feet per minute prior to the crash, NBC News reported .

Four adults and two boys, ages 8 and 10, were on board, Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros said.

Air traffic control in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45 p.m. CT that it had lost contact with the plane, officials said.

A search effort was launched by the Coast Guard and federal, state and local partner agencies. Rescue efforts were called off after roughly four hours when officials located the remains of all six people within the fuselage of the aircraft.

"This is a heartbreaking outcome, and our deepest sympathies are with the families and loved ones who are facing an unimaginable loss," Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard sector mobile search and rescue mission coordinator , said.

"While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

Horn Island is 12 miles long and the east end is around eight miles from Pascagoula, Mississippi. It is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.

The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will investigate.

articles.title: Dumfries toilet block could be replaced by shipping containers
articles.summary: The brightly-coloured units would replace a block being taken down as part of a £68m flood scheme.
articles.body:
Brightly-decorated shipping containers could be used to replace a toilet block which is being demolished to make way for a multi-million pound flood scheme.

The building on the Whitesands in Dumfries is being taken down to allow new protection measures to be put in place next to the River Nith.

Plans have been lodged to put shipping containers in the New Bazaar car park on the opposite side of the road to replace the present provision.

An application said the proposals would help meet sustainability goals and could either be sold on or relocated to a new location if required.

The flood defence scheme work has started in Dumfries and it will see a long-standing set of toilets demolished.

A supporting statement said the solution in the town centre conservation area could "inject some colour and breathe life into the area".

"There are converted shipping containers located in close proximity of the car park that have been used as extensions of local businesses therefore, we believe this temporary solution would not be out of place," it said.

"Black containers could be painted with coloured murals to allow the toilets to be visible from both the Whitesands and Friars Vennel and pays homage to the previous use of the car park as an event space for the Big Burns Supper.

"Due to the finish of the structures being painted steel there are opportunities for collaboration with community groups and artists to incorporate murals or sign painting onto the finished structures."

An application for the plan said the containers could be painted a variety of colours and required little maintenance.

It added that converted containers would "retain their value over time".

"Containers could be easily removed from site and relocated for use elsewhere such as local events in the future," it said.

articles.title: Trump’s Russia business pitch loses steam as Putin presses for Donbas: Report
articles.summary: The Trump administration has quietly pushed business deals with Russia to the sidelines of its efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Financial Times
articles.body: The Trump administration has quietly pushed business deals with Russia to the sidelines of its efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Financial Times reported.US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff told European officials that corporate partnerships were no longer central to Washington’s pitch to Moscow, with negotiations now focused on territorial and security issues, the FT reported, citing five officials briefed on the shift.In recent months, Kushner and Witkoff had floated postwar proposals including US investment in Russian oil and titanium projects, the resumption of pipeline gas sales to Europe and the restoration of US airlines’ access to Russian airspace. The ideas were intended to offer Russian economic incentives to end his full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Russian officials initially welcomed the prospect of business deals, viewing them as a way to keep Trump engaged in negotiations. But Moscow has since shown little interest in the proposals, as it continues to demand territorial concessions from Kyiv that Ukraine has rejected.During the latest round of talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, Russian officials reportedly focused on their demands rather than economic cooperation, making clear they were not interested in side deals to soften their position.“The Russians were not in the market for this kind of thing,” one official briefed on the discussions told the FT.A US official disputed the report, saying it was “not accurate” to suggest economic engagement had been dropped.“We are organising our negotiating tracks and will announce them when we are ready and this continues to be an element,” the official said, referring to postwar economic ties with Moscow.Another official described the economic proposals as “on the back burner”, adding that Washington had shifted towards a more traditional negotiation focused on “land for peace”.Kushner’s public statement on the negotiations on Sunday also appeared to emphasise a potential postwar security arrangement rather than economic incentives.Putin has said he is prepared to end the war if Ukraine gives up the entirety of the eastern Donbas region. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly rejected the demand, while senior Ukrainian officials have warned that territorial concessions may not satisfy Moscow’s ambitions.The proposed business ventures had been floated in September as a way to revive stalled peace talks. US officials had said they would only proceed after the war ended.The Kremlin’s apparent lack of interest in the proposals suggests that economic incentives may do little to soften its demands, as negotiations increasingly centre on territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.Putin remains unwilling to accept a deal that does not involve further Ukrainian territorial concessions.You use AI every day. articles.summary: IShowSpeed has managed to beat Kai Cenat in their GTA 6 $1 million challenge after pulling off an incredible comeback.
articles.body: IShowSpeed has managed to beat Kai Cenat in their GTA 6 $1 million challenge after pulling off an incredible comeback. The two streamers went head-to-head to see who could earn $1 million in the game first. Kai looked like he had the win in the bag after taking a $500,000 lead over Speed. However, one unexpected moment changed everything. Even after his PS5 crashed and he struggled to keep up, Speed refused to quit and fought his way back to victory.Kai Cenat loses his $500,000 lead after dying during GTA 6 challengeKai Cenat looked like the easy winner in the early stages of the challenge. The streamer had been able to raise $500,000 more than Speed, giving him a massive advantage in the race to the $1 million mark.But then things went south for Kai when he died in GTA 6. The viral Xl post about the challenge says he died and lost all his progress. This was a golden opportunity for Speed to catch up and take the lead.The unexpected turn of events completely changed the contest. What looked to be a straightforward win for Kai turned into a tough race, with Speed getting a shot to beat his longtime rival.Speed also had a problem of his own during the challenge. articles.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
articles.summary: The draft proposal could see the UK join the scheme without having to increase import taxes on Chinese cars.
articles.body:
The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by European ambassadors later on Wednesday.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Alignment with higher EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles would increase their price in the UK, at a time when they have become increasingly popular.

It also raises the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on cars made in the UK.

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times , is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. After Wednesday's meeting of EU ambassadors, it will be discussed again by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting before Christmas.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

After last week's EU-UK summit in Brussels, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Made in Europe had become a "source of real concern across the British economy, particularly for our car makers".

"It will come as a relief to workers that the UK and EU committed in Brussels to avoid measures that would harm each other's industries," he added.
